Japan does not see one “world.” It sees five different maps.

America can be security and sneakers. China can be civilization, commerce and anxiety. Italy may arrive as pasta before politics. The countries missing from Japan’s opinion polls reveal as much as the countries inside them.

Researched and edited in Japan by Yuji Shimizu · Published October 15, 2026 · Sources checked October 15

Walk into a Japanese supermarket and the world is already on the shelves. American cereal, Australian beef, Philippine bananas, Italian pasta, Moroccan octopus and British tea can sit within a few aisles. Turn on the news and the same places rearrange themselves: the United States becomes an alliance; China becomes an economic giant and maritime concern; Russia becomes war, sanctions and a territorial dispute.

So how does Japan see the outside world? There is no honest one-sentence answer. “Japan” is 124 million individual people, plus institutions, companies, schools and communities with different experiences. A government survey measures one kind of view. A family recipe, a manga set in Europe, a Filipino colleague or a Brazilian-Japanese relative creates another.

A boundary before the ranking. This article describes recurring frames in Japanese surveys, diplomacy, education and popular culture. It does not claim every Japanese person shares them, and it does not turn any country into a personality type. Governments, people and cultures are separate things.

Map one: the countries Japan is asked to judge

The Cabinet Office’s most recent full foreign-affairs opinion survey, conducted in October 2024 and published in March 2025, asked Japanese adults about affinity toward selected countries. The United States scored 84.9% “friendly” or “somewhat friendly.” China scored 14.7%. Russia scored 5.0%. Those gaps are real results from that survey—but they are not a global ranking.

The method changes what the numbers mean. A person can dislike a government policy while loving a language, cuisine or friend from that country. “Affinity” can reflect the news cycle, security concerns and historical disputes. It is not a moral score assigned to citizens.

There is an even bigger trap: Australia, the Philippines, Italy, Morocco and Iraq do not appear beside those three in a complete, comparable league table. Their absence is not evidence of indifference. It means the survey was designed around particular diplomatic questions. What Japan measures most often is frequently what it worries about most.

The reveal is not that Japan likes one nation and dislikes another. It is that Japan uses different instruments to see different parts of the world—and then mistakes those instruments for one map.

America: ally, screen and argument

The United States occupies more layers of Japanese life than any single poll can separate. It is the treaty ally whose military presence is central to Japan’s security and contested intensely in places such as Okinawa. It is also Hollywood, hip-hop, baseball, denim, hamburgers, universities, technology companies and a century of imported vocabulary.

In the 2024 survey, 94.9% said developing Japan–US relations was important for both countries and the Asia-Pacific. That number describes strategic importance, not automatic agreement with Washington. The same person may support the alliance, oppose a base relocation, follow Major League Baseball and distrust a particular American administration. Contradiction is not hypocrisy; it is what a dense relationship looks like.

China and Russia: the closest maps are often the hardest

China is not simply “foreign” in Japan. Chinese writing shaped the Japanese script; Buddhism and statecraft traveled through the continent; trade binds the two economies. At the same time, the Senkaku/Diaoyu dispute, military activity, detentions, food-safety disputes and sharply different accounts of twentieth-century history fill Japanese news. Low affinity toward China’s current image coexists with deep cultural inheritance and daily economic dependence.

Russia sits differently. Japanese literature and music have long engaged Russian culture, and communities around Hokkaido and the Sea of Japan have histories of exchange. Yet Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the unresolved Northern Territories/Southern Kurils dispute dominate the official frame. The 5.0% affinity result captures that severe political moment; it cannot tell us what a reader feels about Chekhov, a musician about Tchaikovsky or a family with Russian relatives.

Australia and the Philippines: partnership enters ordinary life

Australia is often visible in Japan through trust built from repetition: energy, food, tourism, study abroad and security cooperation. In 2026 the two countries mark 50 years since signing the Basic Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation. The relationship has moved far beyond the wartime memory that once defined it, without erasing that history.

The Philippines is even harder to reduce to foreign policy. Japan and the Philippines mark 70 years since normalization in 2026, but the human relationship is present every day in Japanese hospitals, care homes, factories, churches, schools and mixed families. War memory, development assistance, maritime security, migration and pop culture all occupy the same relationship. A Japanese child with a Filipino parent does not experience “bilateral relations” as a headline; it is home.

Britain and Italy: “Europe” arrives as separate rooms

Japanese speech often treats Yōroppa—Europe—as one distant cultural zone. Travel advertising reinforces the collage: castles, cafés, Christmas markets, art museums and football. Yet Britain and Italy occupy very different imaginative rooms. Britain arrives through English education, royal ceremony, rock music, literature, tailoring and Premier League football. Italy arrives through design, Renaissance art, football, fashion, espresso and food that Japan has adapted with extraordinary confidence.

The food shows how admiration becomes local. Napolitan spaghetti is Japanese, despite its Italian name. Japanese “Italian” restaurants can be meticulous about regional pasta and still serve cod-roe spaghetti that makes sense only after ingredients cross borders. This is not failed authenticity. It is evidence that Japan often domesticates the admired foreign thing until it becomes part of its own everyday vocabulary.

The 2024 Japan Foundation survey counted 14,646 learners at Japanese-language institutions in the United Kingdom and 7,117 in Italy. Those figures exclude casual apps and some short programs. They remind Japanese readers that looking is reciprocal: people abroad are also constructing their own Japans through language.

Morocco and Iraq: a country can be familiar in fragments

Morocco may enter Japanese life as octopus, couscous, argan oil, desert imagery or the name of a World Cup opponent before it arrives as a 70-year diplomatic partner. The anniversary in 2026 makes a useful correction. Morocco is not scenery at the edge of “Africa” or “the Arab world”; it is a specific state with long relations, its own languages, cities, institutions and debates.

Iraq carries a heavier media frame. For many Japanese adults, the name recalls the Gulf War, the 2003 invasion, hostage crises and the Self-Defense Forces’ reconstruction mission in Samawah. Those memories can make an entire society appear only through conflict. Yet Iraq is also Mesopotamian heritage, universities, families, contemporary art and ordinary ambitions. Responsible curiosity begins by noticing when war reporting has crowded civilian life out of the picture.

The same correction applies in reverse: being known through food or beauty can flatten people just as conflict can. A flattering stereotype is still a stereotype. “Romantic Morocco” and “dangerous Iraq” both erase internal variety.

Map four: the continent labels hide unequal knowledge

“Africa” is 54 UN member states, yet Japanese conversation often uses the continental label where it would name Italy, Britain or France individually. The Foreign Ministry’s 2026 Diplomatic Bluebook devotes a major feature to TICAD 9, the Japan-led conference on African development, showing that official engagement is far more detailed than popular familiarity. Business, public health, climate, education and cultural exchange do not fit one safari-or-aid image.

South America and the Caribbean are also closer to Japan than the map suggests. Japanese migration created large Nikkei communities, most famously in Brazil but also in Peru, Argentina, Paraguay, Bolivia and elsewhere. The Foreign Ministry now describes Latin America and the Caribbean through supply chains, food and mineral security, democracy, climate cooperation and those human networks—not only distance.

The Caribbean can disappear inside the acronym LAC, even though island states face distinctive climate and ocean challenges. Japan’s relationship with CARICOM includes disaster resilience and maritime concerns familiar to another island country. The useful comparison is not “small islands versus Japan,” but how societies surrounded by water manage exposure, connection and limited resources.

Map five: what Japanese words reveal

The Japanese word 海外, kaigai, literally means “beyond the sea.” It can mean overseas or abroad. The geography inside the word is revealing: Japan’s outside begins by crossing water. 外国, gaikoku, is a foreign country; 外国人, gaikokujin, is a foreign national or foreign person. In ordinary speech, the softer loanword gaijin exists too, but it can sound distancing depending on context and speaker.

Kaigai makes Los Angeles and Lagos equally “beyond the sea,” even though Japan’s connections to them are radically different. Language compresses distance. History expands it again. That is why the most honest answer to “How does Japan see my country?” begins with another question: through which map—security, school, food, family, travel, memory or media?

How to read Japan’s view without being reduced by it

If your country appears negatively in a Japanese poll, remember what was measured and when. If it appears only through cuisine or tourism, look for the less visible relationship: students, migrants, trade, local sister cities, disaster relief or art. If an entire region is named as one block, ask which countries and people have vanished inside the label.

Japan’s image of the world is incomplete, sometimes anxious and sometimes beautifully curious. So is every country’s image of everywhere else. The goal is not to produce a kinder stereotype. It is to replace the stereotype with more doors.

Walk Japan LIVE with Yuji and you can see those doors in ordinary streets: Filipino groceries, British pubs, Italian cafés, Chinese temples, Brazilian festivals and words borrowed from several languages. DraMap—Yuji’s iOS game—lets learners notice how Japanese itself stores encounters with the outside world.

A poll tells you which countries are on the questionnaire. Daily life tells you which countries are already inside Japan.
